title: Reproduce the bug
plain: To reproduce a bug is to make it happen again on purpose, with exact steps and input. A minimal reproduction is the smallest program or steps that still show the same failure.
check: A friend says 'my app sometimes crashes'. Which three facts do you need from them before anyone can start fixing it?
rubric: Asks for the exact steps or command and the input used before the failure.
Asks for the full error message, copied and not described, and what the friend expected to happen instead.
Asks about the environment (operating system, language version, the file or data used) and how often it happens.
try:
In a scratch folder create report.py with these lines:
scores = {"ada": 90, "grace": 85}
names = list(scores)
print("Names:", names)
total = sum(scores.values())
print("Total:", total)
average = total / len(scores)
print("Average:", average)
best = max(scores, key=scores.get)
print("Best:", best)
print("Third place:", names[2])
print("Done")
Run python report.py (python3 on macOS and Linux). It prints several lines, then fails with IndexError: list index out of range, pointing at line 10. Write down the command and the last line of the error. Now create small.py with only two lines: names = ["Ada", "Grace"] and print(names[2]). Run it: the same error, with nothing else around it. small.py is the minimal reproduction.
pitfall: Wrong belief: changing code until the error goes away is debugging. Correct: without a way to make the bug happen on demand you cannot know that a change fixed it; make it fail every time first, then change one thing at a time.

title: Read the error message
plain: An error message says what failed and where. In Python, the last line gives the error type and reason; the traceback above it lists the files and line numbers that led there.
check: A traceback ends with NameError: name 'totl' is not defined. What do you check first, and what probably happened?
rubric: Names the error type from the last line: NameError.
Gives the file name and the line number from the traceback.
Explains in plain words that the name totl was never defined, and checks for a spelling mistake against the real name (total).
try:
In a scratch folder create oops.py with two lines:
names = ["Ada", "Grace"]
print(names[2])
Run python oops.py (python3 on macOS and Linux). You see 'Traceback (most recent call last):', a line with the file name and 'line 2', the code line print(names[2]), and last: IndexError: list index out of range. Read the last line first, then line 2. The list has 2 items, at positions 0 and 1, so position 2 does not exist.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a long error message means I broke something and only an expert can read it. Correct: the last line says what happened and the lines above say where, and most fixes start there.

title: Print debugging
plain: Print debugging means adding lines that print values, such as variable contents or a message, while the program runs, so you can see what really happens and compare it with what you expected.
check: Your program prints 555 where you expected 15. What single value would you print to find out why, and what do you hope to learn from it?
rubric: Writes a prediction before the first run
Prints the value and its type, with type() or repr()
Explains that text multiplied by 3 repeats the text
try:
In a scratch folder create amount.py with two lines:
amount = "5"
print(amount * 3)
Run python amount.py (python3 on macOS and Linux): it prints 555, not 15. Add this line before the print: print(type(amount), repr(amount)). Run it again: the first line is <class 'str'> '5'. The value is text, not a number, so * 3 repeats it. Delete the debug line when you are done.
pitfall: Wrong belief: print lines are a beginner habit that real developers replace with debuggers. Correct: printing is a normal, fast way to see real values; predict first, print one thing at a time, and remove the print afterwards.

title: Find where it broke
plain: Bisecting means finding the change that broke something by halving the search: test the middle, decide if the bug is before or after it, and repeat. Git can do this with git bisect.
check: Your project has 1,000 commits. The newest one has a bug and the oldest one does not. About how many commits must you test to find the first bad one, and why that few?
rubric: Says about 10 tests, because each good or bad answer halves the range and 2 to the power 10 is 1,024.
Runs git bisect start, marks the newest commit bad and an old commit good, and answers good or bad at each commit Git offers.
Reads the line '<hash> is the first bad commit' (here the commit change 6) and ends with git bisect reset.
try:
Needs Git with your name and e-mail already set. In a new empty folder that is outside any project, create make_history.py:
import subprocess
for n in range(1, 9):
    status = "ok" if n < 6 else "broken"
    with open("value.txt", "w") as f:
        f.write("step %d: %s\n" % (n, status))
    subprocess.run(["git", "add", "value.txt"], check=True)
    subprocess.run(["git", "commit", "-q", "-m", "change %d" % n], check=True)
Run: git init -b main, then python make_history.py (python3 on macOS and Linux). Then run git bisect start, git bisect bad, git bisect good HEAD~7. Git checks out a middle commit and prints 'Bisecting: 3 revisions left to test after this (roughly 2 steps)'. Show the file with python -c "print(open('value.txt').read())": if it says ok, type git bisect good; if it says broken, type git bisect bad. Repeat until Git prints '<hash> is the first bad commit' and the commit is 'change 6'. Finish with git bisect reset.
pitfall: Wrong belief: to find the commit that broke things, I must read every commit. Correct: each good or bad answer halves the range, so a long history needs few tests; commit or stash your own changes first so the checks stay clean.

title: Unit tests
plain: A unit test runs one piece of your code with a known input and uses an assertion to check the result. If the result is not the expected value, the test fails.
check: A test that passed yesterday fails today, and you only changed the function. What are the two possible explanations?
rubric: Says one explanation is that the change broke the behaviour: a real bug that the test caught.
Says the other is that the behaviour was meant to change, so the expected value in the test is out of date.
Reads the failure message, which shows the expected and the actual value, to decide which case it is, and does not edit the test only to make it pass.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if all my tests pass, the code is correct. Correct: it proves only that the cases you wrote work, and a weak assertion, such as only checking that a result exists, proves very little.

title: Run the tests
plain: The test suite is all the tests of a project. You run it with one command, such as npm test or python -m pytest, and read how many tests passed and failed.
check: All tests passed before your change. After it, two tests fail. What does that tell you, and what do you do first?
rubric: Says the change most likely caused the two failures, because every test passed before it.
Reads the names of the two failing tests and the message for each before editing anything.
Fixes one thing at a time, runs the two tests again, then runs the whole suite and reads the summary line.
try: On your project, look for the test command: in package.json under "scripts" the entry "test" (run it with npm test), or in the README for Python projects (often python -m pytest). Run it once without changing any code. Expect a summary such as '3 passed'. No tests yet? In a scratch folder that holds test_price.py from the unit test card, run python -m unittest (python3 on macOS and Linux): it finds files named test*.py by itself and prints 'Ran 1 test' and OK.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if the test suite passes, the app works. Correct: it shows only that the tests that exist pass, so check how many tests actually ran and what they cover.

title: Regression tests
plain: A regression test is a test that captures a bug you fixed. It fails on the broken code and passes on the fixed code, so the bug is caught if it ever returns.
check: You fixed a bug and tried the app by hand: it works now. Why is adding a test still worth the extra minutes?
rubric: The test uses the exact input that triggers the bug
The test fails before the fix and shows the wrong result or error
The test passes after the fix and the older tests still pass
pitfall: Wrong belief: a bug that is fixed stays fixed. Correct: later changes, including changes made by an AI assistant, can bring it back, and a regression test is what notices without you checking by hand.

title: Manual test checklist
plain: A manual test checklist is a short written list of things to do in your app by hand, each with the result you expect. You run it after important changes and before sharing.
check: Your todo app checklist has the line 'add a task'. Which two more lines would you add so the list tests more than the normal path, and what result do you expect for each?
rubric: Each line has an action and an expected result
The list includes the main path and at least one unusual input
Every line was run and marked pass or fail
try:
In your project create CHECKLIST.md. Write one line per check, in the form 'action -> expected result'. For a todo app:
1. Open the app -> the page loads and the Console (F12) shows no red errors
2. Add the task "buy milk" -> it appears in the list
3. Add an empty task -> nothing is added and nothing crashes
4. Reload the page -> the task is still there (only if the app is meant to save tasks)
5. Delete "buy milk" -> it disappears
Run the steps by hand and write pass or fail after each line. Every fail already contains the steps to report it.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if I clicked around once and it worked, it is tested. Correct: you repeat the steps you always take and skip the others; a written checklist makes the test repeatable and records what you actually checked.

title: Linters and formatters
plain: A linter reads your code without running it and warns about likely mistakes, such as an unused variable or a missing name. A formatter rewrites the layout so spacing and quotes are consistent.
check: A linter reports no problems in your file, but the app shows the wrong total. Why is that possible, and which kind of tool would catch it?
rubric: Says a linter looks for risky patterns and style problems and cannot know what the right total is.
Names tests, such as a unit test with a known input and the expected total, as the tool that catches a wrong result.
Can read one linter report: the rule code (for example F401), the file, the line and the explanation.
try:
Install Ruff once if you do not have it (ask Claude to help; the command is python -m pip install ruff, best inside a virtual environment, and it downloads a package, so Claude will ask first). In a scratch folder create unused.py with two lines:
import os
print("hi")
Run ruff check unused.py. Expect a report that names the rule F401, says `os` is imported but unused, and points at unused.py line 1 (the layout differs between Ruff versions), followed by 'Found 1 error.' and a note that --fix can repair it. Nothing in the file changes unless you add --fix.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a linter or formatter makes my code correct. Correct: a linter flags patterns that are often mistakes and a formatter only changes layout; neither can tell whether the program does what you want, and tests do that.

title: The debugger
plain: A debugger pauses your program at a chosen line so you can look at the variables and run it one line at a time. In Python, breakpoint() starts the built-in debugger, pdb.
check: At the (Pdb) prompt, total is 4 and the next line is total = total + price, where price is 10. What will total be after you type n, and how can you confirm it without the program's own print?
rubric: The program stops and shows a (Pdb) prompt
Uses n to run one line and p to print a variable
States the value of total before and after one loop step
try:
In a scratch folder create cart.py:
prices = [4, 10, 6]
total = 0
breakpoint()
for price in prices:
    total = total + price
print("Total:", total)
Run python cart.py (python3 on macOS and Linux). The program stops and shows a (Pdb) prompt and an arrow -> that marks the line it will run next. Type n and press Enter until the arrow points at total = total + price (the arrow may start on the breakpoint() line itself, depending on the Python version). Type p price (prints 4), p total (prints 0), then n and p total again (prints 4). Type c to continue: it prints Total: 20. Type q instead of c to quit at any time.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the debugger finds and fixes the bug for me. Correct: it only pauses the program and shows its state, and you still decide what is wrong; remove breakpoint() before you commit, or the program stops and waits for input.

title: Edge cases
plain: An edge case is an unusual but valid situation, such as empty input, zero, a very large number, a single item or special characters, where code often breaks.
check: A form asks for a person's age. Which four inputs could a real user type that are not the normal case, and what do you want the app to do with each?
rubric: Lists at least four different edge inputs
Writes a prediction for each before running
Runs them and marks where the code crashed or surprised
try:
In a scratch folder create edges.py:
def first_word(text):
    return text.split()[0]


print(first_word("hello world"))
print(first_word(""))
Run python edges.py (python3 on macOS and Linux). The first line prints hello. The second call ends the program with IndexError: list index out of range, because an empty text has no first word. Decide what the function should return for empty text (for example an empty string) and change the code.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if it works with my example, it works. Correct: your example is the normal case you were thinking about; bugs hide at the edges (empty, zero, one, many, very large), which are cheap to try.

title: It works on my machine
plain: 'It works on my machine' means the program works for you but fails elsewhere because the environment differs: other versions, missing packages, different settings or files, or a different operating system.
check: A friend clones your repository and gets ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests', though the program runs for you. What is the most likely cause, and where should the fix live?
rubric: Says requests is installed on the first computer but is not listed in the project's dependency file (requirements.txt or pyproject.toml).
Puts the fix in the project: add the dependency to that file, and say in the README how to install and run the project.
Proves the fix by cloning into a new folder, setting up a fresh environment and following only the README.
try: From inside your project (it needs at least one commit) run: git clone . ../fresh-copy. This creates a new folder next to your project and changes nothing in it. Open the new folder and run the project the way your README says. The fresh copy contains only committed files, so anything missing, such as .env, a package that is not listed, or a change you never committed, shows up as an error. You can remove the fresh-copy folder when you are done.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if it runs on my computer, the code is fine. Correct: your computer has things nobody else has, such as installed packages, a .env file and your versions; a fresh clone is the proof that counts.
